name: Chuj
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: The vowels of Chuj are high and low front vowels i and e, low central a and low and high back rounded vowels o and u. Strong stress in words is generally on the vowel of the root, with secondary stress on final syllables. While marking stress is not part of the official orthography and is not necessary for native speakers, in other works—and in the text analysis below—I have added accent marks on the strong syllables to help the nonnative reader appreciate the rhythm of speech.
new_statements.citation: Hopkins, Nicholas A. 2021. Chuj (Mayan) Narratives: Folklore, History, and Ethnography from Northwestern Guatemala. Louisville: University Press of Colorado. Appendix I, 'A Short Sketch of Chuj Phonology, Grammar, and Syntax'. DOI 10.5876/9781646421305.
new_statements.locator: Appendix I, p. 127 (PDF p. 136); cf. p. 126 on stress/contour/juncture and Appendix II pp. 146ff. where line 2 of the text analysis marks stress
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: (OAPEN open-access UPC monograph; present listing 8 files -> citations -> URLs). extracted text of PDF p.136 (book p.127, Appendix I 'A Short Sketch of Chuj Phonology, Grammar, and Syntax') gives exactly: 'The vowels of Chuj are high and low front vowels i and e, low central a and low and high back rounded vowels o and u. Strong stress in words is generally on the vowel of the root, with secondary stress on final syllables. While marking stress is not part of the official orthography and is not necessary for native speakers, in other works—and in the text analysis below—I have added accent marks on the strong syllables to help the nonnative reader appreciate the rhythm of speech…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (strong) word stress falls on the root vowel (typically the first syllable of the lexical stem, after any prefixes/proclitics), with a secondary stress on the word-final syllable; stress is not contrastive and not written in the ALMG orthography. Hopkins's own stress-marked transcriptions (Appendix II) show this: kálnel, yík'ti7al, k'úhalil (root k'uh + -al-il), mám kícham, with final marks in péká7, 7ókés, kaníh.
new_statements.exceptions: Noun classifiers are unstressed when functioning as determiners but stressed when used pronominally (p.129-130); incorporated object nouns in the -w-ih antipassive are obligatorily unstressed (p.137; dictionary 2012 p. xi [stúk.wi.ch'al.wính]); directional suffixes occur in an unstressed set (+5) and a stressed set (+6) (p.132); stress on noun classifiers inside fossilized classifier+noun compounds varies (p.138). COMPETING FIRST-HAND STATEMENT: ALMG Gramática normativa Chuj (Domingo Pascual 2007:81, saved): 'En el idioma Chuj el acento no cambia el significado de las palabras y no se marcan. En algunas palabras tienen acento grave pero la mayoría de las palabras tienen acento agudo por eso no se tildan.' [= stress is non-contrastive; most words are final-stressed, some penultimate] -- a brief native-speaker normative statement that reads as predominantly FINAL stress, plausibly reflecting the final (secondary/phrase-final) prominence Hopkins also notes; Q'anjob'alan relatives show phrase-conditioned initial-vs-final stress (Bennett 2016 sec. 6.1).
new_statements.domain_note: Hopkins's statement is about the word ('Strong stress in words'); his fuller 1967 treatment reportedly handles stress together with contour and juncture (phrase-level) phenomena, and his text transcriptions mark stress in running narrative, not citation forms. The ALMG statement concerns isolated words. Variety: San Mateo Ixtatán Chuj for Hopkins; ALMG covers the Comunidad Lingüística Chuj (San Mateo Ixtatán and San Sebastián Coatán).
new_statements.identity_note: Hopkins's description is of San Mateo Ixtatán Chuj (fieldwork 1964-65; Glottolog dialect 'San Mateo Ixtatán Chuj' under chuj1250). The ALMG 2007 grammars are issued for the whole Comunidad Lingüística Chuj (San Mateo Ixtatán and San Sebastián Coatán varieties). No source examined distinguishes the two dialects with respect to stress.

sources.locator: Appendix I, p. 127 (PDF p. 136); cf. p. 126 on stress/contour/juncture and Appendix II pp. 146ff. where line 2 of the text analysis marks stress
sources.note: p.127: 'Strong stress in words is generally on the vowel of the root, with secondary stress on final syllables'; stress not part of official orthography; Hopkins adds acute accents on strong syllables in the Appendix II text analysis (e.g. kálnel, yík'ti7al, k'úhalil, kaníh, péká7), and notes noun classifiers are unstressed as determiners/stressed as pronouns, incorporated objects unstressed, and directional suffixes come in unstressed vs stressed sets. Refers to Hopkins 1967 diss. (and its AILLA modernized version) for the full treatment including 'stress, contour, and juncture phenomena'.

sources.citation: Bennett, Ryan. 2016. Mayan phonology. Language and Linguistics Compass 10(10): 469-514 (author preprint).
sources.note: Sec. 6.1 surveys Mayan stress (final in K'ichean, phrasally conditioned initial/final in Q'anjob'al, Popti', Akatek, Tojolab'al etc.) but gives no Chuj-specific stress statement; cites Hopkins 1967 only for segmental facts.

sources.citation: Domingo Pascual, Pascual Martín. 2007. Stzolalil Stz'ib'chaj Ti' Chuj / Gramática normativa Chuj. Guatemala: Academia de Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala (K'ulb'il Yol Twitz Paxil). 298 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 2.4.3 'Acento', p.81: 'En el idioma Chuj el acento no cambia el significado de las palabras y no se marcan. En algunas palabras tienen acento grave pero la mayoría de las palabras tienen acento agudo por eso no se tildan.' (i.e. stress non-contrastive; most words final-stressed ['agudo'], some penultimate ['grave']); examples Mak'a', Ixwayi, Ixchami without marking.

sources.citation: Royer, Justin, Rodrigo Ranero, Pedro Federico Felipe Gómez & Diego Neper Josué López García. 2025. The tale of the kokolom/chi'jolom: Grammar sketch and dialectal comparison of the Chuj language (San Mateo Ixtatán vs San Sebastián Coatán). lingbuzz/009030, 104 pp.
sources.note: No mention of stress/acento (grep of full text for stress|acento|accent|prosod finds only bibliography titles).

sources.citation: Royer, Justin, Pedro Mateo Pedro, Elizabeth Carolan, Jessica Coon & Matal Torres. 2020 [Tlalocan 27, 2022]. Atz'am k'ik' atz'am: The story of Xuwan and a grammatical sketch of Chuj. lingbuzz/005630, 48 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 2.1 'Orthography and basic phonological properties' covers inventory, <w> allophony, <h>, glottal stop; mentions prosodic conditioning of status suffixes (phrase-final) but says nothing about word stress placement.

sources.citation: Buenrostro Díaz, Elsa Cristina. 2013. La voz en Chuj de San Mateo Ixtatán. Tesis de doctorado, El Colegio de México, Centro de Estudios Lingüísticos y Literarios. 303 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 3.1 'Aspectos fonológicos' (pp.106-108) gives consonant/vowel inventories, no phonemic length, syllable structure; explicitly not an exhaustive phonology; silent on stress/acento.

sources.citation: Hopkins, Nicholas A. 2012. A Dictionary of the Chuj (Mayan) Language as Spoken in San Mateo Ixtatán, Huehuetenango, Guatemala, ca. 1964-65. Tallahassee: Jaguar Tours (FAMSI online). 437 pp.
sources.note: No general stress rule; introduction p. xi notes that in object-incorporating antipassives the incorporated noun is unstressed, with phonetic form [stúk.wi.ch'al.wính]; scattered entries repeat this.

sources.citation: Comunidad Lingüística Chuj. 2007. Gramática pedagógica del idioma maya Chuj. Guatemala: ALMG. 228 pp.
sources.note: p.23 'd) Acentuación': words are not orthographically accented but carry 'acento prosódico' on the syllable pronounced with most force; examples K'alem, sikila', Machtak given without indicating which syllable -- no position rule stated.
